about: The common Preface — the shortest of the Roman prefaces and the only one that names no mystery: it says merely “through Christ our Lord” and goes straight to the angels. The choirs it names — Angels, Dominations, Powers, Virtues, Seraphim — come from the New Testament lists (Col 1:16; Eph 1:21) and from Isaiah's vision. The whole stretch from nos tibi to ágere is an infinitive clause — that we should give You thanks — hanging from the short est near the beginning.

s01.narrative: The priest parts his hands and holds them apart to the end of the Preface.

s02.translation: It is truly right and just, our duty and our salvation, always and everywhere to give You thanks:

s03.translation: Lord, holy Father, almighty and eternal God: through Christ our Lord.

s04.translation: Through Him the Angels praise Your majesty, Dominions adore and Powers tremble before You.

s05.translation: Heaven and the Virtues of heaven and the blessed Seraphim worship together with exultation.

s06.translation: May our voices, we pray, join with theirs in humble praise, as we acclaim:

w002.function: The priest repeats the words of the answer just made — Dignum et iustum est — and adds two of his own.

w005.function: The only finite verb in this long sentence; everything from nos down to ágere is its subject, with æquum and salutáre as predicates.

w006.function: The received English prays “our duty and our salvation” for æquum et salutáre — a sense-rendering; the glosses keep the words' own senses.

w008.function: The neuter of the adjective salutáris, not the noun salutáre (salvation): it stands in a series with dignum, iustum and æquum.

w009.function: The accusative subject of the infinitive “ágere” (w015) — a construction English renders with a that-clause.

w015.function: The infinitive depending on “est” (w005): it is a worthy thing that we should give.

w021.function: Six words of address at once — only the Gloria runs longer.

w025.function: Here the common Preface stops without naming any mystery; the proper prefaces put into this place whatever the day commemorates.

w027.function: The relative reaches back to Christ and opens the relative period that carries the Preface to its end.

w028.function: One object for three verbs: they praise it, adore it, tremble before it.

w033.function: Nominative, not accusative: the subject of adórant, not a second object of “laudant” (w030). The form is the same in both cases; the three parallel verbs decide it.

w036.function: Cælum takes a masculine plural — cæli, not cæla; it is a noun that changes gender in the plural.

w037.function: A genitive depending on “Virtútes” (w038): the Virtues belonging to the heavens.

w040.function: Neuter plural, because Latin treats the indeclinable Séraphim as a neuter plural.

w042.function: An ablative of manner with “exsultatióne” (w043), not a nominative with the subjects.

w046.function: No gender is given: the antecedent is the whole heavenly host, made of nouns of more than one gender, and the form marks none.

w049.function: The accusative subject of the infinitive “admítti” (w051); “iúbeas” (w052) governs the whole construction.

w052.function: A subjunctive after ut; the petition is put as a wish rather than a command.

w053.function: A deponent: passive in form, active in meaning. It stands in mid-sentence like a parenthesis.

w055.function: A confession not of guilt but of praise — what the Sanctus is about to sing.

w056.function: The participle agrees with the unstated “we”; the sentence breaks off, and the Sanctus is its continuation.
